newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Fresh lease on power for Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Fresh lease on power for Milosevic.

text.p: Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic won a fresh lease on power on Tuesday when the federal parliament elected him president of Yugoslavia in an adroit transfer from his expiring Serbian presidency.
The ruling Serbian and Montenegrin Socialist parties pushed his unopposed nomination through both chambers of parliament with comfortable majorities that swamped isolated protests.

Milosevic, a 55-year-old former communist who has dominated Yugoslav politics for a decade, was expected to refashion the ceremonial federal presidency as the centre of executive power once he is sworn in on July 23.
Elected president of Serbia twice since 1990, he was forbidden by the constitution from seeking another term at the end of this year.

Milosevic's switch to the federal post was the first hurdle in a strategy to rebuild his authority after street protests earlier this year against election fraud and a public feud with Montenegro, Serbia's smaller partner in the Balkan federation.
His ex-communist Socialist party (SPS), which has held power since the end of World War Two, still has to fight Serbian parliamentary and presidential elections before the end of the year.
An election to succeed Milosevic in the Serbian presidency must be held within two months.

Opposition hopes of breaking the Socialist stranglehold have faded since February, when a coalition of opposition parties backed by international pressure forced Milosevic to recognise their victories in Belgrade and other main cities in local elections.
But the coalition has since collapsed amid the rival claims of its leaders to power.

More dangerous to Milosevic personally has been a dispute with leaders of Montenegro who accused him of thwarting their efforts to rebuild the southern republic's economy after the lifting of U.N. sanctions.
The Montenegrin Socialist party, the DPS, reluctantly agreed to back Milosevic for the federal presidency but refused to let him change the constitution to officially strengthen its powers.

Yugoslavia's economic revival from sanctions has been stalled by Milosevic's resistance to U.S.-led pressure to promote democratic reforms and to handing over war crimes suspects wanted for trial by the United Nations.
He has also failed to deliver a settlement with the ethnic Albanian majority seeking autonomy in Serbia's southern province of Kosovo.
The United States has retaliated by keeping Yugoslavia out of international diplomatic and financial institutions.
